front: On a married person's death, what does the surviving spouse already own?
back: One-half of the community property and one-half of the decedent's quasi-community property (Prob. Code §§ 100, 101). That half never enters the estate.

front: What property may a married testator dispose of by will (§ 6101)?
back: His or her separate property, one-half of the community property, and one-half of his or her own quasi-community property.

front: Is out-of-state land quasi-community property at death?
back: No. At death QCP includes personal property wherever located and California real property only (§ 66); land in another state passes under the situs state's law.

front: Elements of QCP recapture under § 102.
back: Decedent domiciled in CA; QCP transferred to a non-spouse without substantial consideration and without the spouse's written consent or joinder; decedent retained possession/income, a power to revoke or invade, or a survivorship interest. Survivor may compel restoration of one-half.

front: Does California have an elective (forced) share for a surviving spouse?
back: No. Protection comes from community property, QCP and recapture (§§ 100–102) and the omitted-spouse statute (§ 21610).

front: Spouses die together with no proof of order. What happens to their CP?
back: One-half is administered as if it belonged to each spouse and that spouse survived, so each half passes through that spouse's estate (§ 103).

front: How is a surviving spouse's waiver of death rights made enforceable (§§ 142–143)?
back: In writing and signed by the surviving spouse; enforceable unless the survivor proves no fair and reasonable disclosure (not waived after independent advice) or no independent counsel at signing.

front: What is the § 144 fallback for a spousal waiver that fails § 143?
back: The court enforces it if (1) it made a fair and reasonable disposition of the survivor's rights when signed, or (2) the survivor had or should have had adequate knowledge of the decedent's property and the decedent did not breach Fam. Code § 721(b) — unless enforcement would be unconscionable (§ 144(b)).

front: How can a contract to make a will (or not revoke) be proved under § 21700?
back: (1) Will/instrument states its material terms; (2) express reference plus extrinsic evidence; (3) writing signed by decedent; (4)–(5) clear and convincing evidence of an agreement or promise enforceable in equity (to claimant or for claimant's benefit).

front: Do mutual (mirror) wills create a presumption of a contract not to revoke?
back: No (§ 21700(b)). The contract must be proved by a § 21700(a) method.

front: What survival standard applies to beneficiaries under a will in California?
back: Clear and convincing evidence of survival (§§ 220, 222; § 21109). The 120-hour rule applies only to intestate heirs (§ 6403).

front: Joint tenants die simultaneously. Result?
back: Property divided equally; each share administered as if that joint tenant survived (§ 223).

front: Insured and beneficiary die; no proof the beneficiary survived. Result?
back: Proceeds distributed as if the insured survived the beneficiary (§ 224), so they go to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate. Special rule for a CP policy with no alternative beneficiary: see R-WIL-010.

front: Describe California's default representation under § 240.
back: Divide at the first generation below the ancestor that has a living member: one share per living member and per deceased member with living issue; deceased members' shares drop to their issue the same way.

front: What does 'per stirpes' in a will mean in California?
back: Strict per stirpes under § 246: divide at the children's generation even if all children are dead.

front: Slayer rule: who is barred and how is it proved?
back: A person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent takes as if predeceased; JT severed. Final conviction conclusive; otherwise preponderance in probate (§§ 250–254).

front: When is an elder abuser treated as predeceased (§ 259)?
back: When proven by clear and convincing evidence liable for physical abuse, neglect or financial abuse of the elder/dependent-adult decedent and acting in bad faith or with recklessness, oppression, fraud or malice (or convicted of specified crimes).

front: Effect of a valid disclaimer?
back: The disclaimed interest passes as if the disclaimant predeceased the decedent (§ 282); a disclaimer within nine months is conclusively presumed timely; after that the disclaimant must prove the time was reasonable (§ 279).

front: What property passes by intestacy (§ 6400)?
back: Any part of the estate not effectively disposed of by will — the whole estate if no valid will, or the failed part. Nonprobate property and the survivor's CP half are excluded.

front: Surviving spouse's intestate share of CP and QCP (§ 6401)?
back: The decedent's half of the CP (so the spouse has all CP) and the decedent's half of the decedent's QCP.

front: Surviving spouse's intestate share of SP (§ 6401(c))?
back: All if no issue, parent, sibling or issue of a sibling; one-half if one child (or issue of one) or no issue but a parent or parent's issue; one-third if more than one child, one child plus issue of a deceased child, or issue of two or more deceased children.

front: Is a spouse in a pending divorce a 'surviving spouse'? A legally separated spouse?
back: Pending divorce: yes. Legal separation: yes only if the judgment did not terminate all marital property rights; a party to an order ending all marital property rights is not a surviving spouse (§ 78(d); Estate of Lahey).

front: Order of heirs under § 6402 after the spouse's share.
back: Issue → parents → issue of parents → grandparents or their issue → issue of a predeceased spouse → next of kin → parents of a predeceased spouse or their issue → escheat (§ 6404).

front: Unmarried D dies leaving a child and both parents. Who inherits?
back: The child takes everything; parents take only if there is no issue (§ 6402).

front: What is § 6402.5?
back: If decedent leaves no spouse or issue, property from a spouse who died within 15 years (real) or 5 years (personal) passes first to that predeceased spouse's relatives.

front: 120-hour rule (§ 6403).
back: An intestate heir must survive the decedent by 120 hours, proven by clear and convincing evidence, or is deemed predeceased — unless that would cause escheat. Not applicable to wills.

front: Half-blood relatives in California intestacy?
back: Take the same share as whole-blood relatives (§ 6406).

front: Child in utero at the parent's death?
back: Inherits as if born in the parent's lifetime (§ 6407). Posthumously conceived children need § 249.5 compliance.

front: When is a lifetime gift an advancement (§ 6409)?
back: Only if the decedent declared it so in a contemporaneous writing or the heir acknowledged it in writing.

front: Advancee predeceases. Is the advancement charged to the advancee's issue?
back: No, unless the declaration or acknowledgment provides otherwise (§ 6409(d)).

front: Debt an heir owes the decedent?
back: Charged against that heir's intestate share, but not against the issue of a debtor-heir who predeceased (§ 6410).

front: Does a child of unmarried parents inherit from the father?
back: Yes. Parent-child relationship exists regardless of the parents' marital status (§ 6450(a)), once parentage is established (§ 6453).

front: Effect of adoption on inheritance from natural parents (§ 6451)?
back: Severed unless (1) the natural parent and child lived together as parent and child at any time (or parent died before birth while married to/cohabiting with the other parent) AND (2) adoption was by a natural parent's spouse or after a natural parent's death.

front: Can the natural parent's family inherit from an adoptee under § 6451(b)?
back: Generally no (except whole-blood siblings and their issue), unless the adoption was by the natural parent's spouse or surviving spouse.

front: Three grounds that bar a parent from inheriting from a child (§ 6452).
back: Parental rights terminated (not reestablished); parent did not acknowledge the child; or parent left the child during minority without an effort to support, or without communication, for 7+ consecutive years through minority, with intent to abandon.

front: When does a stepchild inherit from a stepparent (§ 6454)?
back: Relationship began in the child's minority and continued through joint lifetimes, AND clear and convincing evidence that the stepparent would have adopted but for a legal barrier.

front: Estate of Joseph (1998) holding on § 6454.
back: The legal barrier to adoption must persist until death, not just during minority — so a natural parent's refusal that ends at majority does not qualify.

front: Equitable adoption elements (Estate of Ford).
back: Intent to adopt (express or implied agreement, may be oral) and conduct consistent with it, proved by clear and convincing evidence; a close relationship alone is not enough (§ 6455).

front: Small-estate affidavit threshold for deaths on or after Apr 1, 2025?
back: $208,850 (§ 13100); a primary residence up to $750,000 may pass by petition (§ 13151).

front: Who may make a will in California?
back: An individual 18 or older and of sound mind (§ 6100).

front: Three-part testamentary capacity test (§ 6100.5).
back: At execution, ability to understand (1) the nature of the testamentary act, (2) the nature and situation of the property, and (3) relations to descendants, spouse, parents and those affected by the will.

front: Insane delusion under § 6100.5(a)(2).
back: A mental health disorder with delusions or hallucinations that cause a disposition the testator would not otherwise have made; only the affected gifts fail.

front: Who bears the burden in a will contest (§ 8252)?
back: Proponent: due execution. Contestant: lack of testamentary intent or capacity, undue influence, fraud, duress, mistake or revocation.

front: Can a conservatee make a will?
back: Yes, if he or she meets § 6100.5 at execution; a conservatorship does not remove the right (§ 1871(c)).

front: When may a conservator make a will for a conservatee?
back: Only under a court order of substituted judgment (§ 2580); the conservator signs (§ 6110(b)(3)); a competent conservatee may revoke it (§ 6100).

front: Does a will pass property acquired after it was signed?
back: Yes. A will passes all property owned at death, including after-acquired property (§ 21105).

front: Effect of undue influence on a will (§ 6104)?
back: Execution or revocation is ineffective to the extent procured by duress, menace, fraud or undue influence — only the tainted provisions fail.

front: Define undue influence.
back: Pressure on the testamentary act that overcomes free will and substitutes the influencer's wishes (Rice v. Clark); § 86 adopts W&I § 15610.70: excessive persuasion overcoming free will resulting in inequity.

front: Four § 15610.70 factors for undue influence.
back: Victim's vulnerability; influencer's apparent authority; actions or tactics used; equity of the result.

front: Elements of the common-law presumption of undue influence (Rice v. Clark).
back: (1) Confidential relationship; (2) beneficiary actively participated in procuring the will; (3) undue benefit. Burden of proof shifts to the proponent.

front: Fraud in the execution vs fraud in the inducement.
back: Execution: testator deceived about the nature or contents of the document. Inducement: knowing misrepresentation intended to and actually influencing the disposition.

front: Remedy when fraud prevents a testator from revoking a will.
back: The will stands; a constructive trust is imposed on the wrongdoer's gain.

front: Duress vs menace.
back: Duress: force or threats coercing the act. Menace: threat of injury to the person, property or character of the testator or family. Both void the procured provisions (§ 6104).

front: 'Since I'm flying tomorrow, I leave all to my sister.' Condition or motive?
back: Usually read as motive, so the will is effective even if the testator dies later of other causes; § 6105 conditions must be clear from the will's terms.

front: When is extrinsic evidence admissible to interpret a will?
back: Provisionally, to decide whether language is reasonably susceptible to more than one meaning, and if so to resolve it (Estate of Russell; §§ 6111.5, 21102).

front: Constructional preferences in §§ 21120–21122.
back: Give every expression effect; prefer constructions avoiding intestacy; read all parts together; ordinary meaning of words.

front: Estate of Duke (2015) rule on reformation.
back: An unambiguous will may be reformed on clear and convincing evidence of (1) a mistake in expression of intent at drafting and (2) the testator's actual specific intent.

front: Requirements of an attested will (§ 6110).
back: Writing; signed by testator (or by another in presence and at direction, or conservator by court order); two witnesses present at the same time who witness signing or acknowledgment, understand it is the testator's will, and sign during the testator's life.

front: Must California witnesses sign in the testator's presence?
back: No. They must be present together when the testator signs or acknowledges, and sign during the testator's lifetime.

front: Harmless-error rule (§ 6110(c)(2)).
back: A will not executed with proper witnessing is treated as valid if clear and convincing evidence shows that, when the testator signed, he intended it to be his will.

front: Can § 6110(c)(2) save an unsigned typed will?
back: No. It cures only witnessing defects; the writing and the testator's signature are still required.

front: Interested witness rule (§ 6112).
back: Will valid; unless two other disinterested witnesses, a gift to a witness raises a presumption of duress, menace, fraud or undue influence (burden of proof); if unrebutted, the witness takes no more than the intestate share.

front: Does § 6112's presumption apply to a witness named as executor?
back: No — not where the gift is made solely in a fiduciary capacity.

front: Holographic will requirements (§ 6111).
back: The signature and the material provisions are in the testator's handwriting; witnesses unnecessary; testamentary intent may appear in a printed form.

front: What are 'material provisions' of a holograph?
back: Who takes what: the beneficiaries and the property given.

front: When is an undated holograph invalid (§ 6111(b))?
back: If inconsistent with another will unless shown to be later; or if the testator lacked capacity at any time it might have been executed, unless shown to have been executed while competent.

front: § 6111.5 extrinsic evidence.
back: Admissible to decide whether a document is a will under § 6110 or § 6111, and to determine its meaning if unclear.

front: Choice of law for execution (§ 6113).
back: Valid if executed per the law of the place of execution at that time, the law of domicile/abode/nationality at execution or death, or California law.

front: California statutory will witnessing.
back: Two witnesses; § 6221 requires each to sign in the testator's presence (no longer in each other's presence). Defective forms may survive as attested wills or holographs.

front: Handwritten interlineation on a typed attested will: when effective?
back: Only if it qualifies as a holographic codicil — material provisions and a signature in the testator's handwriting.

front: Integration doctrine.
back: Papers present at execution and intended to be part of the will are integrated, shown by physical connection or internal coherence.

front: Effect of republication by codicil.
back: The will is treated as executed on the codicil date — can defeat omitted spouse/child claims, allow incorporation of later writings, and validate a defective earlier will.

front: Incorporation by reference elements (§ 6130).
back: Writing in existence when the will was executed; will manifests intent to incorporate; describes it sufficiently to identify it.

front: § 6132 tangible personal property writing requirements.
back: Unrevoked will refers to it; dated; in testator's handwriting or signed; reasonable certainty; total ≤ $25,000 and no item > $5,000; may be written before or after the will.

front: Two § 6132 writings conflict. Which controls?
back: The most recent writing.

front: Acts of independent significance (§ 6131).
back: A will may refer to acts or events with significance apart from the will (e.g., 'my employees at my death'), before or after execution or death.

front: Current pour-over rule (§ 6300).
back: Devise to the trustee of a trust identified in the will, with terms in an instrument executed before, concurrently with, or within 60 days after the will; valid though unfunded, amendable or revocable; amendments apply.

front: Trust revoked before the testator dies. Effect on the pour-over?
back: The devise lapses unless the will provides otherwise (§ 6300).

front: Beneficiary dies before the testator; default result?
back: The gift lapses (§ 21109) unless anti-lapse applies; a gift to a person dead at execution is void but anti-lapse can still apply.

front: California anti-lapse (§ 21110): who is protected?
back: Kindred of the transferor or of the transferor's surviving, deceased or former spouse; their issue take by representation.

front: Does anti-lapse protect a predeceased spouse or a friend?
back: No. Neither is kindred of the testator.

front: Is 'to my brother if he survives me' a contrary intent under § 21110?
back: Yes. A survivorship requirement is a contrary intention; the brother's issue do not take.

front: Order for a failed non-residuary gift (§ 21111).
back: Alternative disposition in the will → residue → estate (intestacy).

front: One of two residuary beneficiaries predeceases (not saved by anti-lapse).
back: The share passes to the other residuary beneficiary (§ 21111(b)); no 'residue of a residue' intestacy.

front: Class gift: one class member predeceases.
back: Surviving members share, unless anti-lapse substitutes the member's issue; members dead at execution and known to the testator are excluded.

front: Are adopted persons and stepchildren included in 'grandchildren'?
back: Per intestacy rules (§ 21115(a)); a person adopted by someone other than the transferor counts only if raised as a minor in the adopting parent's household (§ 21115(b)).

front: Define specific, general, demonstrative and residuary gifts (§ 21117).
back: Specific: identifiable property. General: from general assets. Demonstrative: general gift payable primarily from a named fund. Residuary: what remains.

front: California approach to ademption by extinction.
back: Specific gift adeemed if the item is gone, but a traceable change in form does not adeem absent intent (Estate of Mason); statutory exceptions apply; § 21139 disfavors ademption.

front: What does § 21133 give a specific beneficiary when the item is sold, condemned or damaged?
back: Unpaid purchase-price balance, unpaid condemnation award, unpaid insurance or recovery, and property acquired by foreclosure on a specifically given secured obligation.

front: Specific gift of 100 shares; 2-for-1 split. Result?
back: Beneficiary takes 200 shares; issuer-initiated changes follow the gift (§ 21132).

front: When does a lifetime gift satisfy a testamentary gift (§ 21135)?
back: Will provides for deduction; testator's contemporaneous writing; beneficiary's written acknowledgment; or the gift is the same specifically given property.

front: Specific devisee of mortgaged land; will says 'pay my debts.' Exoneration?
back: No. A specific gift passes subject to liens without exoneration despite a general debt-payment clause (§ 21131).

front: Conservator sells specifically devised house. Beneficiary's right (§ 21134)?
back: A general pecuniary gift equal to the net sale price, unreduced by payoff of encumbrances the conservator placed on it; not if the conservatorship ends and the testator survives a year.

front: Order of abatement (§ 21402).
back: (1) Intestate property; (2) residuary; (3) general to non-relatives; (4) general to relatives; (5) specific to non-relatives; (6) specific to relatives. Pro rata within each class.

front: How does a demonstrative gift abate?
back: As a specific gift to the extent the designated fund is available, and as a general gift for any balance.

front: Two ways to revoke a will under § 6120.
back: (a) A later will revoking expressly or by inconsistency; (b) burning, tearing, canceling, obliterating or destroying with intent, by the testator or another in the testator's presence and by direction.

front: Lawyer destroys the will at his office on the testator's phone instruction. Revoked?
back: No. Proxy revocation must be in the testator's presence and at the testator's direction.

front: Does California allow partial revocation by physical act?
back: Yes — 'a will or any part thereof' (§ 6120(b)). Added words still need holographic or attested execution.

front: Will executed in duplicate; testator tears one with intent.
back: The will is revoked (§ 6121).

front: § 6124 lost-will presumption.
back: Will last in testator's possession, testator competent until death, will and duplicate not found → presumed destroyed with intent to revoke; presumption affects only the burden of producing evidence.

front: Effect of divorce on a will (§ 6122).
back: Revokes gifts, powers of appointment and fiduciary nominations to the former spouse unless the will provides otherwise; read as if the ex-spouse predeceased; revived by remarriage to the ex.

front: Does § 6122 revoke a gift to the ex-spouse's mother?
back: No. It reaches only provisions for the former spouse (contrast UPC § 2-804).

front: Does legal separation revoke gifts to the spouse under § 6122?
back: No. Only dissolution or annulment that ends surviving-spouse status.

front: POD account naming an ex-spouse after divorce (§ 5040).
back: Fails as if the ex predeceased, unless not revocable, clear and convincing intent to preserve, or a court order; ERISA plans follow federal law.

front: Revival when the revoking will is revoked by physical act (§ 6123(a)).
back: The first will is revived only if the circumstances of the revocation or the testator's contemporaneous or subsequent declarations show intent that it take effect.

front: Revival when the revoking will is revoked by a third will (§ 6123(b)).
back: Only to the extent the terms of the third will show intent that the first will take effect.

front: Dependent relative revocation.
back: A revocation based on a mistaken belief that another disposition is valid is disregarded if giving effect to the revoked will or gift is closer to the testator's intent (Estate of Kaufman).

front: T crosses out '$10,000 to Nick,' writes '$20,000,' no signature. Result?
back: $20,000 fails (no holographic signature); strike-out is a partial revocation, but DRR restores the $10,000.

front: Omitted spouse share (§ 21610).
back: Decedent's one-half of CP, one-half of decedent's QCP, and SP equal to the intestate share but not more than one-half of the SP.

front: Timing requirement for an omitted spouse.
back: Married the decedent after the execution of ALL testamentary instruments (will, codicils, revocable trust).

front: Exceptions to the omitted spouse share (§ 21611).
back: (1) Intentional omission appearing in the instruments; (2) provision outside the will intended in lieu (statements, amount, other evidence); (3) valid waiver; (4) AB 328: spouse was the care custodian of a dependent-adult decedent who died within 6 months of the marriage, unless the spouse proves no fraud or undue influence by clear and convincing evidence.

front: Is 'I disinherit anyone not named in this will' enough to defeat a later spouse?
back: No — a general clause not mentioning the spouse or a future marriage does not show intent (Estate of Shannon).

front: How is an omitted spouse's or child's share funded (§§ 21612, 21623)?
back: First from property not disposed of by will or trust, then pro rata from all beneficiaries by value at death; court may adjust to preserve the plan.

front: Do the omitted-heir statutes apply to revocable trusts?
back: Yes. 'Testamentary instruments' include a revocable trust, and the 'estate' includes trust property (§ 21601).

front: Omitted child share (§ 21620).
back: A child born or adopted after all testamentary instruments receives the share he or she would take if the decedent died intestate.

front: Three exceptions to the omitted child share (§ 21621).
back: (1) Intentional omission on the face of the instruments; (2) decedent had a child and left substantially all to the omitted child's other parent; (3) transfer outside the will intended in lieu.

front: Child alive when the will was signed but left out. Claim?
back: None, unless omitted solely because the decedent believed the child dead or did not know of the birth (§ 21622).

front: When is a no-contest clause enforced (§ 21311)?
back: Only against a direct contest brought without probable cause, and — if the clause expressly says so — a challenge to the transferor's ownership or a creditor's claim.

front: Probable cause for a will contest (§ 21311(b)).
back: Facts known to the contestant would cause a reasonable person to believe there is a reasonable likelihood the relief will be granted after further investigation or discovery.

front: Grounds that make a pleading a 'direct contest' (§ 21310).
back: Forgery; lack of due execution; lack of capacity; menace, duress, fraud or undue influence; revocation; disqualification under §§ 6112, 21350 or 21380.

front: Who is a presumptively disqualified donee (§ 21380)?
back: Drafter; fiduciary who transcribed or caused transcription; care custodian of a dependent adult (instrument within service period ± 90 days); care custodian who married or cohabited with the dependent adult (transfer within 6 months); their close relatives, cohabitants, employees and law-firm colleagues.

front: How is the § 21380 presumption rebutted?
back: By clear and convincing evidence that the transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence — except it is conclusive for the drafter and drafter's associates; loser pays costs and fees.

front: Main exceptions to § 21380 (§ 21382).
back: Relatives within the fourth degree or cohabitant; instrument drafted by such a person; court-approved instrument; public entity or charity; gifts ≤ $5,000 from estates at or above the § 13100 amount; out-of-state nonresident instrument.

front: Certificate of independent review (§ 21384).
back: Independent attorney counsels the transferor outside the presence of beneficiaries, tries to detect fraud or undue influence, and signs the certificate; then § 21380 does not apply.

front: Unpaid long-time friend provides care. Care custodian?
back: Not if the personal relationship began at least 90 days before services, 6 months before death and before hospice (§ 21362).

front: Effect when a § 21380 gift fails (§ 21386).
back: The instrument operates as if the beneficiary predeceased without spouse, domestic partner or issue — anti-lapse cannot save it.

front: Must a POD designation or trust meet will formalities?
back: No. § 5000 validates nonprobate transfers in listed written instruments without will formalities.

front: Does a will reach joint tenancy property?
back: No. It passes to the surviving joint tenant by survivorship, even between spouses who bought it with CP (Brace left survivorship at death intact), subject to the slayer and former-spouse rules, a § 852 written transmutation, and QCP recapture.

front: 'Mom in trust for Ben' account — who takes at Mom's death?
back: Ben, the Totten trust beneficiary, unless clear and convincing evidence of a different intent (§ 5302).

front: Revocable TOD deed formalities.
back: Capacity; signed, dated, notarized; two witnesses (deeds on or after Jan 1, 2022); recorded within 60 days; revocable; effective at death.

front: Can a will change a life insurance beneficiary?
back: Generally no — the contract controls unless it allows change by will.

front: Tort of intentional interference with expected inheritance.
back: Recognized (Beckwith v. Dahl) where independently tortious conduct defeats an expectancy and no adequate probate remedy exists.

front: PRC bridge: how does California's intestate order differ from the PRC first order?
back: PRC: spouse, children and parents share first order. California: spouse share depends on survivors; parents take only if no issue (approx.).

front: PRC bridge: Does California have a necessary share (必留份) for dependent heirs?
back: No. Protection is via CP, the omitted-spouse and omitted-child statutes (approx.).

front: Essay structure for 'What rights do A, B and C have in T's estate?'
back: Threshold (law, characterization, validity of will) once; then claimant by claimant: rights under will, statutory claims, intestacy; end with shares in numbers.

front: Pour-over trust signed 45 days after the will. Valid?
back: Yes under current § 6300 (within 60 days after the will).

front: Gift of '$10,000 from my Chase account'; the account is closed before death. Adeemed?
back: No. It is a demonstrative gift (§ 21117(c)), paid from general assets if the named fund is gone; only specific gifts adeem. A gift of 'my Chase account' itself would be specific.

front: Is a notary an acceptable substitute for a witness?
back: No. A notarized but unwitnessed typed will fails § 6110(c)(1), though § 6110(c)(2) may still save it.
